doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

chapter: Boston, Berklee and the band family
title: Wally's Cafe in Boston and learning the form
summary: Weekly gig at Wally's where older rhythm sections tested him; advice to know the form of a tune.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Definitely. Also to find people to come to play with. Also all throughout that I was playing several other types of gigs like wedding gigs and, you know, working at this place called Wally’s in Boston, it was like a weekly gig for me, Wally’s Café. And that was sort of a school outside of the school. That’s where everyone got — you know you hear stories about the jazz clubs where Charlie Parker got a cymbal thrown at him. It’s that type of place where you kind of honed your chops and if you couldn’t play the band would suck. Like I would go in and try and play “Night in Tunisia” or some type of — and I thought I could play over it. But then all of a sudden one by one they left. If you couldn’t hack it, that’s how you get your chops I guess.
Because the rhythm section was older players?

They were older players, familiar with every standard in the Real Book and had been playing it for the millionth time. So here I come, young Sam, thinking I could, it just happened to everybody too. And then you had to be able to cut it, basically. So that was Wally’s experience. It’s like real life experience, getting punched in the face. And then
you’re like okay, I’d better go practice. I’d better go play this again if I ever set foot in there again. And then, you know, I just kept on playing in the Boston scene a lot.
If you were going to tell a student, in relation to that experience, “You better know the tune.” What do you need to know about the tune?

You need to know the form, especially that. Because a lot of people in the beginning would forget A-A-B-A. You think it’s the simplest thing in the world, but you go back to A after the first B, done. Make sure you know the form. Play over it. Solo over it as many times as you can and listen to it over and over and over again, and hear where the tune’s going to go. Don’t go back to the top. It’s like you think it’d be easy, but in the heat of the moment when you’re like maybe stressed and worried and things like that, you forget and then whoops.
It’s interesting, on some of those songs like “So What” or something, it’s A-A-B-A, except because the chords are so simple you can mess it up.
Yeah, yeah, yeah exactly. Or “Impressions,” it’s the same thing.
